shortDescription: See what competing sites publish and find topics worth exploring. Confirm search limits, available data and export options before you buy.
description:
BuzzSumo Group Buy is an option to compare if you need content ideas, examples from competitor websites or a way to track mentions. The most useful place to start is a question from your audience. Look at how other publishers have answered it, see what readers responded to and decide what your own page can explain more clearly.

BuzzSumo offers tools for content discovery, research and monitoring. The features and limits you can use depend on the access you choose. If you need a particular date range, alert type or report export, confirm it before ordering. That makes it easier to judge the offer against the work you actually need to do.

Find ideas from a topic you already understand

Write down a topic your customers ask about. A small business software company might start with invoice reminders. Search for examples and compare the kind of content that appears. You might see templates, guides, opinion posts or case studies. Group the examples by what they help a reader do.

Look for an unanswered question rather than copying the most popular title. If many articles explain when to send a reminder but few show what a friendly reminder looks like, write a useful example. If an article is popular because it cites a recent event, check whether that event still matters. A topic can attract interest for reasons that do not apply to your audience or publishing date.

Study a competitor's content with a consistent method

Pick a competitor that serves readers similar to yours. Search for its domain and narrow the time period. Save a few pieces that match your audience and offer. For each one, record its topic, format, date and the visible engagement measure. Add a short note about the question it answers.

Repeat the same process for another competitor using the same filters. A broad publisher may get more attention than a specialist site because it has a larger audience. The comparison is more useful when you examine similar formats over the same period. Look at the material itself, including the examples, the depth and the next action it gives the reader.

Read engagement alongside the context

An engagement number can help you decide what to look at next. It cannot explain why a post did well on its own. A useful checklist may be shared widely because it saves readers time. A news item may attract attention because it was published at the right moment. A surprising title may bring reactions even if the page is thin.

Read the piece and consider the audience, format and timing. Compare a few results on the same topic. If several practical guides do well, look for the feature they share, such as an example readers can adapt. If one result is far ahead of the rest, check whether it is tied to a major announcement or widely known brand before you use it as a benchmark.

Turn one finding into a content brief

Write a working title and describe the reader in one sentence. Say what they should be able to do after reading. Add three or four questions the piece must answer. For a guide to sending invoice reminders, that might include when to send the first message, what to say, what details to include and when to follow up.

Use the competitor examples to check what is already covered. Add a useful detail that fits your experience, such as a sample email for a client who has asked for more time. Identify the claims you need to verify and the examples you can produce yourself. This turns a list of links into a brief someone can actually write from.

Build a small content calendar

Choose topics with different jobs. One page might answer a basic question, another might compare options and a third might help a reader complete a task. A mix gives people several ways into your site and gives you a way to link articles that build on each other.

For each topic, write down the audience, format and person responsible. Use a short time range if you want to respond to a current event. For a guide you expect to use for several months, review whether examples, statistics and screenshots are still useful. Keep a note of why you picked each idea so you can judge it against the original goal after publishing.

Monitor brand mentions with useful filters

If the offer includes monitoring, decide what you need to track. Start with your brand name, product names or a topic where new coverage matters. Common words can create noisy results. A local design agency with a generic name may need to add another term that helps distinguish it from businesses with the same name.

Check a few examples before relying on notifications. Decide what needs a response and who will handle it. A relevant review may go to customer support, while a press mention may belong in a monthly report. If you need several alert rules or team delivery, check which options are available under the offer and how results reach you.

Plan a report before you rely on exports

Decide what the reader of the report needs to know. A client may want three content opportunities and a short reason for each. A research teammate may need links, date filters and notes about which metrics were visible. Pick the fields you need before you collect a large set of results.

Ask whether you can export the results or whether you need to record a small sample manually. If exports are available, check the format, row limit and what metrics are included. Save your search filters with the report. That makes it possible to repeat the research later and explain why the results changed.

Compare BuzzSumo Group Buy offers with a sample task

Choose a task you would do in a normal week. For example, compare coverage of a topic across two competitor domains, find three pieces published in the last six months and save links to them. If you need alerts, include one exact alert you want to set up. Ask each provider about those tasks.

Compare search limits, history, access duration and report options. Check whether the data you need is available at the frequency you need it. If an offer is part of a wider package, list the tools you will actually open during the month. Browse the group buy SEO tools catalog if you are comparing content research with keyword research, writing and design tools.

Use content research and keyword research together

Content research helps you see what publishers wrote and how audiences responded on the channels being measured. Keyword research helps you understand the phrases people search for and the answers that appear in search results. Use both when you choose an article topic. Start with the reader’s question and check whether the pages they find already answer it well.

For example, an article about product photography might get strong attention on social platforms because it includes beautiful images. A searcher may be looking for a simpler answer about how to photograph an item using a phone. A useful search article can show the setup, settings and a finished image. The popular example gives you inspiration, while the search question helps you decide what to teach.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use BuzzSumo to find trending topics?

It can help you find examples of content receiving attention around a topic. Check the available discovery features and date filters for the offer you are considering. Review the publish dates and read the examples. If a topic has a short window of interest, decide whether you can publish a useful response while it still matters.

Does high engagement mean a page will rank in Google?

Engagement and search position measure different things. Look at what people search for, what the results show and which questions the current pages leave open. Use engagement to find examples worth studying. Use search evidence and the quality of your answer to decide how you will structure the article.

Can I research a competitor by its domain?

Check whether domain search is included and how the results are grouped. Some sites publish under several subdomains or sections. Confirm that you are looking at the part of the site that serves the readers you want to reach. Compare relevant pages before drawing a conclusion about the entire domain.

Can I export the content research?

Check the exact offer for export formats and limits. If a report needs a certain date range, link field or engagement measure, ask about that field before buying. For a small project, a short list of hand-reviewed examples may give the client a clearer answer than a large download with no explanation.

What should I do if a brand alert returns too many results?

Review the first set of results and note what makes irrelevant examples different. Add a distinguishing phrase if the feature supports it, such as a location or product category. Test the filter again before using it in a client report. Keep a note of the rule and adjust it when the brand launches a new product or changes its name.

Is BuzzSumo useful for a small site?

It can be useful if you publish often enough to apply what you learn. Pick a topic where you already have experience and can add a real example. If your site only needs a few pages, compare the cost and time of using the tool with the research you can do by reading relevant results and talking to customers.

How do I avoid copying competitors?

Write down the question, format and gap you found. Then put the examples away and build an outline around your own experience and evidence. If you refer to a specific fact or finding from another publisher, give credit and link to the source. Use an example you created so the reader can see what your page adds.

Bring the research into your next article

Choose one audience question and gather a small set of examples. Write a brief that explains what the reader should get from your page. Decide what you can show, measure or explain that helps the reader take the next step. Use AnswerThePublic to explore related questions and Frase to organise your outline.

Review the results after publishing

Record the date, topic and reason you chose the article. After it has had time to reach readers, check the evidence that matches your original goal. A guide meant to answer a common search may need a review of Search Console queries. A post designed for an email audience may need a look at clicks and replies. Use those results to decide whether to improve the article, write a related guide or try a different angle.

Example research brief for a local service business

A web design studio wants to reach local shops that have outgrown their first website. Start with a question a shop owner might ask, such as how to tell when a site needs a rebuild. Look for content from other studios, software providers and small business publishers. Note whether each page is aimed at a shop owner or a developer. Those readers may search for similar terms and need different answers.

After reading the results, select two or three common issues you can demonstrate. You might show a confusing mobile menu, a booking form that takes too many steps and a product page that hides delivery details. Create your own examples using a sample site or approved client material. Explain the effect of each problem and how an owner can check it on their phone.

Before adding the topic to your calendar, write down what makes your version useful. The studio might include a five-minute walkthrough someone can do before talking to an agency. Set a simple goal, such as attracting enquiries that mention a specific issue from the guide. That gives you a better way to evaluate the article than comparing its social reactions with those of a much larger publisher.
